name: Maya Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on response at Harbour Road station on the east side, mostly nights with C team. We start at ten with a briefing, then my crewmate Bisi and I take whatever the control room throws at us: domestics, fights outside the bars on Quay Street, a missing teenager, a shoplifter the security guard's been sitting on for an hour. I like the people part, talking someone down on their front step. What wears me out is the paperwork at five in the morning, typing up a statement on a tablet I can't stand.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you can't stand the tablet. What's wrong with it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It freezes, it logs me out, and every form wants twenty boxes ticked before it'll save. I still write everything in my paper pocket notebook first, then copy it across, which the younger lot think is mad. My paper notebook has never crashed in court.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like most of the tech the force has bought so far. Lots of promises in a slideshow, then a tablet that freezes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, mostly to my team in the canteen. I'd probably also say the money spent on AI pilots should have gone on more officers on nights, because we run with four cars for the whole east side some weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't change my life much, and I'm relieved. My worries stay the same ones: we're short-staffed, I'm doing overtime I didn't ask for, and our rent on the flat went up again in September. Jonas, my partner, is a nurse in the emergency department, so we're both on shifts and both tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am, keep the notebook, keep doing my nights. I'd push the officers' association to fight the overtime rota, because that's what actually hurts us. And I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, maybe 150, because three months of savings isn't much if one of us gets hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly flat, a bit worn down. Nothing new to fear, but the old tiredness doesn't go anywhere either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a bad week of overtime look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I did three twelve-hour nights, then got held on for a stabbing scene until eleven in the morning. Jonas was going out the door as I came in, and we didn't eat a meal together for six days. That's the real cost of short staffing, not anything a computer does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the routine tasks did get automated, which ones would you notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the crime number forms and the property logs. I wouldn't mind a machine doing those, as long as I don't have to learn some new system to make it happen. Every new system means another two-day course and a month of everything going wrong.

say: The AI money should have gone on **more officers** for the night shift.
Most police tech so far has been a **slideshow promise** and a tablet that freezes.
think: My life barely changes, and my real worries are **short staffing** and overtime.
Our **rent rise** and two shift-working incomes matter more to me than any software.
do: Keep using my **paper notebook** and working nights with my crewmate Bisi.
Push the **officers' association** to fight the forced overtime rota this year.
Put about **150 a month** into savings to stretch our three-month cushion.
feel: Flat and **worn down**, with no new fear but the old tiredness still there.
S0.quote: Jonas was going out the door as I came in, and we didn't eat a meal together for six days.
fieldNote: Her stress comes from **staffing and rota**, not technology, so a quiet AI world leaves her uneasy, not calm.
She trusts her **paper notebook** over the tablet because it has never failed in court.
Wary of any **new system** because every rollout means courses and a month of errors.

steps.text: Keep working nights with Bisi and writing notes in the paper notebook
Raise the forced overtime rota at the next officers' association meeting
Move 150 a month into savings to stretch the three-month cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and checking, that's half my night after midnight. So this one lands on my desk, not just somebody else's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say AI should do the forms and free us up to be on the street, which is what everyone wants. I'd also say out loud that somebody has to check what it writes, because a statement with my name on it goes to court.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the bosses would use it to cut posts, not to give us time back. If the software writes the file in ten minutes, they'll say five cars can cover what eight did. And I'd be the one stuck, because I've never used these tools and I'm slow with new systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training they force on me, but no more than that. I'd go to every association meeting about it, because the time savings should mean more officers on patrol, not fewer people. And I'd start reading the job ads for the city's community safety team, just to know what else is out there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest. I don't think they'll sack police, but I can see myself becoming the slow one on the team who still writes in a notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably me and Gary, who's been in twenty years and still types with two fingers. The new recruits will pick it up in a week. We'll be the ones getting comments in our reviews about not using the system properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the AI tools on your own, before you're made to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I know that sounds stubborn. I don't trust anything that writes words for me and then my name goes under them. If it gets a time or a description wrong, it's my evidence that gets pulled apart by a defence lawyer.

say: AI should do the **forms** so officers can get back out on the street.
Somebody must still **check every statement** the software writes, because it goes to court.
think: Bosses will use the time saved to **cut posts**, not give it back to patrol.
I'm slow with new systems, so I could become the **slow one** on my team.
do: Do the **compulsory training** on the new report software and nothing beyond it.
Attend every **association meeting** about how the time savings are used.
Read job ads for the city's **community safety team** to know my options.
feel: Anxious about being **left behind** as the officer who still writes in a notebook.
S1.quote: I don't trust anything that writes words for me and then my name goes under them.
fieldNote: The real fear is **fewer posts**, with saved time turned into cuts rather than more patrols.
Refuses to try **AI tools** early, tying that to her name being on evidence in court.
Sees herself and an older colleague as the ones who'll get **bad reviews**.
Looking at **community safety** jobs is a quiet hedge, not a plan she'd say out loud.

steps.text: Sit the compulsory two-day course on the new report-writing software
Argue at association meetings that saved time means more cars on nights
Look through the city council's community safety job ads each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd barely have finished arguing about the tablet. And then robots for the street three years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that you can't police people with a machine, that people on the worst night of their life need a human at the door. I'd be the one posting about it and signing every petition the association puts out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, by 2028 the thinking side of my job is gone: statements, case files, the risk forms for domestics. So I'm a body on the street with a camera until about 2031, then robots come for that too. I'll be thirty-one with no other trade and two years of college that won't count for much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd cut what we spend, no takeaways twice a week, no holiday next summer, and get our savings from three months to six. I'd go to the association and to the local councillor, because there have to be rules about machines arresting people. And I'd talk to Jonas about whether we lean on his job, because a nurse with patients in front of her is safer for longer than a cop writing reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared, more than I'd ever say at work, because I don't have a backup and I'm bad at learning new things fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, I think your job is going to have to carry us for a bit. That's hard for me. I've always paid half of everything since my partner Jonas and I moved in together, and I'd hate it if his nursing job had to carry us. He'd be fine about it, he's kind like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're against the technology, but you'd also be the one living with it. How do you hold both?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, I'm fighting it and I'm also going to be stuck with it. I'd rather fight for rules on how it's used than pretend I can stop it. If robots end up patrolling the east side, I want somebody human deciding who gets arrested.

say: You can't **police people** with a machine when it's the worst night of their life.
I'd sign every **association petition** and post about keeping humans in charge.
think: By **2028** my statements and case files are done by AI, and patrol follows by 2031.
At thirty-one I'd have **no other trade** and a college diploma that counts for little.
do: Cut **takeaways and holidays** to grow our savings from three months to six.
Lobby the association and our **local councillor** for rules on machines arresting people.
Talk with Jonas about his **nursing pay** carrying the household for a while.
feel: Properly **scared**, more than I'd ever admit at work.
Ashamed at the thought of **not paying my half** at home.
S2.quote: I've always paid half of everything since my partner Jonas and I moved in together, and I'd hate it if his nursing job had to carry us.
fieldNote: Sees the **three-year gap** clearly: desk side gone in 2028, street side by 2031.
Her pride in **paying half** at home is the most painful part of the picture.
Fights the technology yet expects to **live with it**, so she aims at rules, not stopping it.

steps.text: Stop the twice-weekly takeaways and skip next summer's holiday
Build savings from three to six months of expenses
Write to the local councillor about rules on machines making arrests
Agree with Jonas that his nursing pay covers rent for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast. But it's not the same panic as two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, that the force needs humans, but I'd say it with a bit more calm. Five years is long enough for unions and councils to set rules, if they get moving now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I've got until 2031 before the report side goes and roughly 2034 before patrol does. That's long enough to do something, but I know myself: I'd put it off for three of those years. The danger for me isn't the robots, it's my own habit of waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself sign up for one thing this year, probably the evening course in youth work at the college, because talking to kids on the estates is the bit of this job I'm good at. I'd keep saving about 200 a month. And I'd stay active in the association, because five years is enough time to win some rules if we fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a bit of room to breathe. Less like a cliff and more like a slope I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why youth work, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring I sat outside the Ferris estate after a call about a runaway. A fourteen-year-old boy who'd run from a care home told me his real name after two hours on a wall, and that night I felt I'd done the job right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you signing up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shifts, mostly, and being tired. The course is Tuesday evenings and I'm on nights half the month. I'd need to ask my sergeant for a fixed rest day, and I hate asking for favours.

say: Five years is enough for **unions and councils** to set rules, if they start now.
The force still needs **humans**, and we have a little time to protect that.
think: Reports go by **2031** and patrol by about 2034, which gives me a window.
My real danger is my **habit of waiting** until the last minute.
do: Sign up for the **evening youth work** course at the city college this year.
Save about **200 a month** while the job is still steady.
Stay active in the **association** pushing for rules on police AI.
feel: Anxious, but with **room to breathe**, like a slope instead of a cliff.
S3.quote: A fourteen-year-old boy who'd run from a care home told me his real name after two hours on a wall, and that night I felt I'd done the job right.
fieldNote: Five years turns her from **fear** to a reluctant plan, but she knows she'll delay.
The **youth work** idea comes from a real night that she's proud of.
Her practical block is the **shift pattern** and her dislike of asking for favours.

steps.text: Enrol in the Tuesday evening youth work course at the city college
Ask the sergeant for a fixed Tuesday rest day to attend classes
Save about 200 a month from her police pay
Keep pushing the officers' association for rules on police AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking AI arrives, and around forty when robots can do patrol.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to get this right, so no excuses. I'd want the association and the government to plan for officers now, not in 2035 when it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels long enough that I'd probably ignore it for a while, and I know that's a bad habit. But it does give me time to finish a proper qualification, maybe in youth work or social work, and still have a career after. At forty I'd be starting again, which is doable but not nice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and my nights for now, but do the youth work course over two years, then maybe a social work degree part-time. I'd keep saving and keep my association membership. Jonas and I might also hold off buying a flat until we know where we'll both be working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say, but not frightened. Ten years is a long time in a job where you don't know what next Friday looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hold off buying a flat. How big a decision is that for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big. We'd been looking at a two-bed near the park for next year. If my job might be gone around 2039 and we'd be paying the mortgage until we're sixty, I'd want to know what I'm doing first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new recruit starting next week, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the job, but get something else on paper alongside it. I'd tell any recruit to finish a degree on the side while the force will still pay for some of it.

say: We've got a **decade** to plan for officers, so there are no excuses.
The association and government should **plan now**, not in 2035.
think: Ten years is long enough that I'd **ignore it** for a while, which worries me.
I could finish a **qualification** and still have a full career after forty.
do: Keep my **night shifts** while studying youth work part-time over two years.
Look at a **part-time social work** degree once the course is done.
Put off buying the **two-bed flat** near the park until our work is clearer.
feel: Uneasy but **not frightened**, since ten years feels like a long time in policing.
S4.quote: I'd tell any recruit to finish a degree on the side while the force will still pay for some of it.
fieldNote: With ten years, her mood drops to **uneasy**, but she admits she might waste the time.
The **flat purchase** is the real household decision tied to this picture.
Advice to recruits shows she values **paper qualifications** she lacks herself.

steps.text: Keep the night shifts on response at Harbour Road for now
Finish the youth work course over two years, then apply for social work
Delay buying the two-bed flat near the park with Jonas

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. I'd have no time, no backup trade, and I'm not quick with new things. What would help is the association winning real rules, like a human decides every arrest, and paid retraining that fits around shift work instead of after it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people we police. If robots and software are watching the east side, the poorest streets will be the most watched, and I'd want someone to ask them what they think.

headlineQuote: My paper notebook has never crashed in court.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old** response officer on nights at Harbour Road station, living with her partner Jonas, a nurse.
She distrusts **new technology** and still writes every note in a paper notebook before typing it up.
Her pressures already exist: **short staffing**, forced overtime and a rising rent on a three-month cushion.
She moves from uneasy to **alarmed** under fast AGI, fearing the loss of her half of the household income.
With more time she'd slowly **retrain** towards youth work, while fighting for rules through the officers' association.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she has no backup trade and learns new systems slowly.
whatWouldHelp: Rules that a **human decides every arrest**, won by the officers' association.
Paid **retraining** that fits around shift work rather than on top of it.
